La historia tiene una injusticia célebre: The history has a famous injustice. The method was published in 1970 by the Finn Seppo Linnainmaa, in his master's thesis, as a general way of accumulating rounding errors; he was not talking about neural networks. Paul Werbos applied it explicitly to networks in his 1974 thesis, and he was not heeded either. The work that made it famous is that of David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams in 1986, in the journal Nature, which showed that with it networks of several layers could be trained and set off the interest that had died with Minsky and Papert's book. Hinton has said many times that they were not the first and that they rediscovered it without knowing.

It reads: “the derivative of L with respect to x is that of L with respect to y, times that of y with respect to x”.

Backpropagating is applying it node by node: each one takes what reaches it from behind, multiplies it by its local derivative, and passes it to the previous one. The local derivative of $+b$ is 1; that of $\cdot w$ with respect to $x$ is $w$ and with respect to $w$ is $x$; that of $\sigma$ is $\sigma(1-\sigma)$; that of $(\,)^2$ is $2e$. All of them sixth-form material.
Se lee: <em>«la derivada parcial de ele:
It reads: “the partial derivative of L with respect to theta is approximately L of theta plus h, minus L of theta minus h, over two h”.

The central version is used —looking at both sides— and not the one-sided one, because its error is of the order of $h^2$ instead of $h$: with small $h$, far more precise.

It is extremely expensive: one evaluation per parameter and per side. It is good for checking, never for training.
Se recorre hacia atrás porque hay muchos: It is traversed backwards because there are many parameters and a single output: one pass gives the gradient of them all at once.

Todo esto lo hacen hoy las bibliotecas s: All this is done today by the libraries on their own, and the technique is called reverse-mode automatic differentiation. It is not symbolic differentiation —no formulas are manipulated— nor numerical —nothing is approximated—: the elementary operations are differentiated exactly and multiplied following the graph. And it is good for much more than networks: it is used in computational physics, in finance to compute portfolio sensitivities, in astronomy to fit orbital models and in structural design, anywhere something has to be differentiated with respect to a great many parameters at once.
